newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Cobalt priced lower, antimony slips.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Cobalt priced lower, antimony slips.

text.p: Pricing operations pressured cobalt lower over the past week, while bouts of Chinese selling ahead of the traditionally slow summer period saw antimony ease in thin trading conditions.

Elsewhere, large movements of molybdenum failed to impact on prices and bismuth calmed after buying activity slowed, though several traders said they would not be surprised if the market sprang back into life in the coming months.
Cobalt, described as fundamentally sound by several traders, fell under pricing.
The move was purely technical and traders believed the pricing operation was instigated by two large European merchants, the trader said.

"The market is being pushed lower for buying opportunities and covering," another trader said. He said that once the pricing has run its course prices could start to climb again. A strike at cobalt producer Inco's Sudbury operation and the continued absence of DLA sales helped to bolster cobalt's fundamentals.
The backdrop of low production from the Democratic Republic of the Congo was also supportive.
However, official data from Zambian cobalt producer ZCCM showed sales in the year to March 1997 had recovered strongly to 5,015 tonnes from a low 2,975 tonnes in the year to March 1996.

Traders noted news earlier this week that Gecamines, the Democratic Republic of the Congo's state mining company, confirmed it was airlifting cobalt from Lubumbashi to Europe to meet a contractual backlog.

In a statement faxed to Reuters, the company's London office said some 200 tonnes of the metal would be handled in this way in June and possibly more in July. "In order to meet contractual backlog, Gecamines confirms having adopted the alternative of airlifting cobalt from Lubumbashi to Europe," the statement said.
Last month, a Gecamines marketing official was quoted as saying the company was airfreighting cobalt to Europe in order to benefit from high prices.
Zambia has also been airfreighting material into Europe.
Traders said most of the material moved was to meet existing contracts.
One trader believed that total combined output from the African producers was likely to be 5,000 tonnes in 1997 from levels of around 10,000 tonnes in 1996.

On the downside a trader said that there were enough units of cobalt around to meet the slow summer requirements and that there may be a move to sell stockpiled Ukrainian material. Currently Russian stockpiled material is coming on to the market.

Chinese selling helped to move the price of antimony lower, though one trader said he expected prices to recover and move higher near-term. "There is good buying on the horizon," the trader suggested.

Floods and subsequent landslides in China had no impact on antimony production, London based traders said. But they are watching and awaiting for further developments following the storm in the central Hunan province.
Movements of large tonnages of molybdenum failed to stir prices.

Traders said despite substantial buying orders from India and Korea they expect prices to maintain current levels. "The buying has been well absorbed and the market remains in good balance," a trader said.
The trader believed around 800 tonnes of metal has been moved.
A recent rise in bismuth slowed as China reduced their offers, sparking some profit-taking from European based traders.

One trader suggested that $4.00 a pound was a psychological cap to the market and discounted recent claims by other market operators that prices had traded above this level. Another trader said he expected prices to move towards $4.50 a pound after a period of consolidation.

Elsewhere, rhodium stabilised after chasing other platinum group metals higher. Traders said the investment fund interest which had kicked life into the market had not been as strong this week following an easing of palladium from 17 year highs of $240.OO an ounce.
